Bucket
bŭk´ět
n. (a vessel for drawing water; the measure Isaiah sets against the nations)
From Old French buquet, a tub, akin to Old English buc, a pitcher. In Scripture the bucket appears twice, and both times it is a figure — once for a nation's overflowing prosperity, once for the weight of all nations before God.

Biblical Definition

Balaam, compelled to bless where he was hired to curse, reaches for the most ordinary thing in a village to say that Israel will not run dry: “He shall pour the water out of his buckets, and his seed shall be in many waters, and his king shall be higher than Agag, and his kingdom shall be exalted” (Numbers 24:7). Isaiah takes the same vessel and uses it for the opposite weighing: “Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance: behold, he taketh up the isles as a very little thing” (Isaiah 40:15). Not a bucket, a drop from one — the film left on the rim that no one bothers to shake off. That is the empires, weighed. The bucket appears again at a well in Samaria, where the woman raises the only objection that occurs to her: “The woman saith unto him, Sir, thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep: from whence then hast thou that living water?” (John 4:11). She is right about the vessel and wrong about the Man. And Jeremiah names the alternative to drawing from God: “For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water” (Jeremiah 2:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a bucket as a vessel in which water is drawn out of a well — made of leather, wood, or iron.

expand to see more

BUCKET, n. [Sax. buc, a pitcher.] A vessel in which water is drawn out of a well; it is nearly in the form of a pail.

BUCKET, n. A vessel for drawing up water from a well, or for holding water, as in a fire-engine.

CISTERN, n. [L. cisterna.] An artificial reservoir or receptacle for holding water, beer or other liquor, as in domestic uses, distilleries and breweries.

BALANCE, n. [L. bilanx.] A pair of scales, for ascertaining the weight of bodies.

DRAW, v.t. To pull along; to haul; to cause to move forward by force; to take water from a well.

Key Scripture

Numbers 24:7 — "He shall pour the water out of his buckets, and his seed shall be in many waters, and his king shall be higher than Agag, and his kingdom shall be exalted."

Isaiah 40:15 — "Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance: behold, he taketh up the isles as a very little thing."

John 4:11 — "The woman saith unto him, Sir, thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep: from whence then hast thou that living water?"

Jeremiah 2:13 — "For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water."

Modern Corruption

Isaiah 40:15 is quoted as though it made human affairs meaningless, when the chapter's point is comfort — the God who weighs empires so lightly carries His lambs in His bosom.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The misuse is pastoral. A believer frightened by the news is told that nations are a drop of a bucket, and hears that nothing matters. Isaiah 40 was written to exiles under the largest empire then alive, and the chapter that weighs the nations at a drop ends with mounting up with wings as eagles. The principle to recover is that the smallness of empires before God is the ground of a Christian's courage, not of his indifference.

Jeremiah 2:13 names the alternative exactly, and it is the more useful verse for ordinary life. The two evils are one motion: forsaking the fountain, and then hewing out cisterns. A cistern is not a sin against good sense — it is a reasonable piece of engineering, and everyone in Judah had one. The sin is preferring stored water to running water, a supply a man controls to a supply he must go to God for. And the cisterns are broken, which is not the prophet's pessimism but simple observation about anything built to replace God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew deli (H1805), a bucket, from dalah, to draw; mar (H4752), a drop; maqor (H4726), a fountain; bor (H953), a cistern.

expand to see more

Hebrew deli (H1805) — a bucket; from dalah, to draw up, Numbers 24:7.

Hebrew mar (H4752) — a drop; Isaiah 40:15, the nations as a drop of a bucket.

Hebrew maqor mayim chayyim (H4726) — fountain of living waters; Jeremiah 2:13.

Hebrew bor nishbar (H953 + H7665) — a broken cistern; the substitute that will not hold.

Greek antlema (G502) — a vessel for drawing; John 4:11, nothing to draw with.

Usage

"“Pour the water out of his buckets” — the promise of a people that does not run dry."

"“A drop of a bucket” — not a bucket; the film left on the rim."

"“Cisterns…that can hold no water” — the reasonable substitute that fails."
